immutable_state.instructions: Does the supplied production code avoid mutable domain state and model state transitions immutably?

criteria.pass: Domain types represent state with immutable properties (`val`) and immutable/defensively-copied collections, and rover transitions return new state rather than mutating fields in place. Local variables inside parsing loops or a fold/loop accumulator holding an immutable value are acceptable.
criteria.fail: Any domain class stores mutable `var` properties, mutates collections/state in place, or shares mutable state across runs or calls.

domain_invariants.instructions: Do the domain types in the supplied production code own and enforce their intrinsic invariants at construction?

criteria.pass: Domain concepts present in the supplied code (such as grid dimensions, coordinates, direction, commands, or rover placement) use dedicated types whose constructors/`init` blocks enforce their validity rules (or are pure enums/value types with no extra validity constraints). Dedicated parser/formatter/entry-point files pass when they delegate domain construction to validated domain types.
criteria.fail: The supplied code passes around raw unvalidated primitives (`Pair<Int, Int>`, unvalidated `Int` dimensions, raw `Char` commands, or raw `String` headings) inside core logic, or enforces domain invariants only in the parser while leaving domain constructors able to create invalid states.

boundary_separation.instructions: Does the supplied production code keep file I/O, text parsing, and output formatting strictly at the boundary, separate from core domain logic?

criteria.pass: File reading (`Path`/UTF-8), line splitting (LF/CRLF), token parsing (`NORTH`/`L`/`R`/`M`/ASCII ints), and output text formatting (`x y direction`) are isolated in dedicated boundary/parser/formatter/entry-point code. Core domain types operate strictly on typed domain values and do not inspect raw strings, characters, line endings, or `Path` objects, nor format output strings.
criteria.fail: Core domain types or movement/grid logic directly read files, parse raw text/characters (`'L'`, `'R'`, `'M'`, `' '`, etc.), or format output strings (`"$x $y $direction"`), OR parsing/formatting logic embeds grid wrapping or rover movement mechanics.

direct_readability.instructions: Is the supplied production code written directly and readably using domain names and explicit domain relationships?

criteria.pass: Names reflect the Mars Rover domain, control flow is straightforward, and domain relationships (such as turning left/right or stepping in a direction) are stated explicitly rather than via clever index arithmetic or cryptic encodings. Focused, clear files pass.
criteria.fail: The code uses clever calculations to encode domain relationships (such as `(ordinal + 3) % 4` for turning), opaque single-letter or generic variable names for domain concepts, regexes where explicit checks are clearer, or convoluted control flow.

modular_organization.instructions: Does the supplied production code organize distinct responsibilities into cohesive, well-scoped types and files rather than dumping everything into one monolithic file or method?

criteria.pass: Each file focuses on one primary type or cohesive responsibility (for example, separating input parsing, output formatting, grid/wrapping, direction, rover execution, and the `MarsRover` entry point; tightly coupled supporting types may stay with their owner), and methods read as clear high-level steps.
criteria.fail: A single file or class jams together multiple distinct responsibilities (such as file I/O, header/command parsing, grid wrapping, rover execution, and output formatting all inside one `MarsRover.kt` file), or packs the workflow into a dense, hard-to-read function.

no_unnecessary_abstraction.instructions: Does the supplied production code avoid speculative interfaces, factories, or pass-through layers?

criteria.pass: Every type, interface, and function serves a concrete role in the phase-one Mars Rover contract without unused interfaces for single implementations, speculative extension hooks, or trivial pass-through wrappers.
criteria.fail: The code introduces speculative interfaces/factories/strategies with a single implementation for hypothetical future commands or formats, or adds pass-through wrapper layers that only forward calls without owning a real responsibility.
